stories.headline: Update: Paraguay's President Peña Impeached Unanimously and Placed Under House Arrest After Bank Collapse
stories.summary:
Paraguay's Senate voted 44-0 on Friday to impeach President Santiago Peña over the collapse of Ueno Bank, which has links to his private business interests. One senator was absent. Peña was arrested minutes after the vote. He had offered to resign on Thursday, but senators declined to accept the resignation and instead impeached and charged him with misconduct. That decision strips him of the immunity usually granted to former presidents.

The charges allege conflicts of interest, manipulation of regulatory oversight, diversion of pension funds, and participation in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank. Peña held shares in the company that owned the bank until last year. He has denied wrongdoing. His lawyer, Ricardo Preda, called the allegations a reckless accusation. Prosecutor Silvia Margarita Gonzalez Vester said Peña is due to be questioned on Saturday over alleged breach of trust, influence peddling and misappropriation of funds.

Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in as interim president and will serve until 2028. He pledged that affected depositors will be fully compensated. An estimated three million depositors remain unable to access their savings and pensions after the central bank seized Ueno, leaving more than half the population cut off from accounts. Protests have spread nationwide, with earlier clashes in which police used tear gas and water cannons.

Senator Rafael Filizzola called the affair the biggest corruption scandal in Paraguay's democratic history. Analysts expect Peña to be prosecuted over the bank's failure. The key questions now are how and when depositors will be repaid and whether the unrest subsides under the new government.

stories.headline: Cornell Faculty Senate Passes No-Confidence Vote Over Handling of Sexual Assault Allegations
stories.summary:
Cornell University's faculty senate voted 75 to 50 on Friday to express no confidence in the central administration's ability to address what it called an ongoing crisis of sexual assault on campus. The vote follows a lawsuit by a former student, identified as Jane Doe, who alleges she was gang raped at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024. The resolution is largely symbolic because the senate cannot remove university leaders.

All seven accused men have denied wrongdoing, and none has been charged. Doe reported the incident to campus police, but the local prosecutor declined to bring charges at the time. She has accused President Michael Kotlikoff of asking why she waited several weeks to report, an account the university says is incorrect.

The board of trustees, which has the power to fire Kotlikoff, said it remains confident in him and his administration. Chairwoman Anne Meinig Smalling said the vote reflects deep anger across campus and that what happened to Doe is unacceptable. Doe's lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, said he believes the senate did not act lightly and hopes the vote helps address the longstanding problem.

Cornell initially defended its disciplinary measures but has since acknowledged it fell short in handling the case. It has hired a former attorney general to conduct an independent review and has announced further measures on assault. Backlash has been intense since Doe filed suit in September.

stories.headline: Dozens of Democrats Weighing 2028 Presidential Bids, Former Obama Campaign Chief Says
stories.summary:
Jim Messina, who ran Barack Obama's 2012 re-election campaign, said more than two dozen Democrats are actively considering 2028 White House runs after the party's strong midterm showing. He told the BBC's Americast podcast he has spoken with over two dozen campaigns that have begun fundraising and hiring staff. He expects exploratory committees to be announced in coming weeks, likely after Thanksgiving.

Messina credited the party's gains to a disciplined focus on the economy and the impact of President Donald Trump's tariffs, which he said hurt rural voters. He said Democrats flipped seats in traditionally Republican states such as Iowa, Kansas and Texas by avoiding what he called social wars. Republicans have not been quoted in this account, and Messina is a partisan Democratic voice whose assessment reflects his own view.

He cautioned that the results were not a ringing endorsement of the party, saying the MVP of the election for Democrats was Trump. He predicted the field could shrink as candidates face the pressure of raising large sums. The harder task, he said, will be uniting the party's progressive and centrist wings in Congress.

Messina said candidates will need a clear economic vision and a position on artificial intelligence, and must decide whether to focus on Trump daily. He called the coming race the most interesting presidential election since 2008.

stories.headline: Jehovah's Witnesses Reverse Blood Transfusion Ban Weeks After Texas Man's Death
stories.summary:
The Jehovah's Witnesses' Governing Body announced a major doctrinal change in September, ending the prohibition on most medical procedures using donated blood. Decisions on such treatments are now left to individual believers. The ban dated to 1945 and rested on interpretations of Bible verses requiring abstention from blood.

The change came 23 days after the death of Isaac Valdez, 26, of Waxahachie, Texas. In August he suffered an epileptic seizure at a library and a resulting brain haemorrhage. As a Witness he carried a No Blood card, and his family honored his wishes when a neurosurgeon said an emergency operation requiring transfusion was the only way to save him. He died on 26 August when life support was withdrawn.

His twin brother, Jacob Valdez, said he is angry that leaders did not reach the decision sooner and believes Isaac could still be alive. Church leaders describe the change as applying Bible principles to modern medicine, though it follows years of pressure from within and outside the faith. The Governing Body is based in New York state.
